category: Myth: the flu shot gives you the flu
stem: It's commonly claimed that 'the flu shot can give you the flu.' Which is the best response based on how flu vaccines actually work?

options.A: False. Most flu vaccines contain killed virus or just antigens, so they cannot replicate or cause infection.
options.B: True. The vaccine contains live flu virus that can replicate in your body.
options.C: True, but only for the live attenuated nasal spray version, which is rarely used now.
options.D: False, but only if you're under 65 years old.

stem: Many large studies (over a million children combined) have examined whether routine childhood vaccines cause autism. What did they find?

options.A: A small but real increase in autism risk after the MMR vaccine.
options.B: Risk only in genetically predisposed children.
options.C: No causal link between routine childhood vaccines and autism.
options.D: Risk only when multiple vaccines are given on the same day.

category: Myth: natural immunity is always better
stem: Compared to a flu vaccine, getting the actual flu produces immunity that is...

options.A: Identical, since both trigger the same B-cell and T-cell response.
options.B: Often broader, but comes with the risks of the actual disease (severe symptoms, complications, sometimes death).
options.C: Always stronger, longer-lasting, and safer than a vaccine.
options.D: Weaker, because the body gives up on memory after fighting a real pathogen.

category: Myth: mRNA vaccines change your DNA
stem: Do mRNA vaccines (such as the COVID-19 vaccines) change your DNA?

options.A: Yes. mRNA gets reverse-transcribed back into DNA inside your cells.
options.B: Only temporarily, until the body finishes making the protein.
options.C: Only in muscle cells, where the vaccine is injected.
options.D: No. mRNA stays in the cytoplasm, is broken down in days, and never enters the nucleus where DNA lives.

category: Myth: half the population is enough (2x payout)
stem: Some claim that 'herd immunity will protect everyone once half the population is immune.' For a highly contagious disease like measles, why is that misleading?

options.A: Because measles is not actually contagious enough to require herd immunity at all.
options.B: Because half-vaccinated populations always reach a stable balance with the disease.
options.C: Because the more contagious a disease, the higher the fraction of the population that must be immune to stop sustained transmission.
options.D: Because herd immunity only works through vaccination, never through natural infection.
